name: V-Sit / Manna
summary: Compression pinnacle after L-sit: V-sit → straddle V → manna. Hip flexor + triceps compression strength.

goal.notes: Straddle manna or advanced V-sit — hips above hands

programming.notes: Pair with wrist + hip flexor mobility. Never train through sharp hip flexor pain.

safety.notes: Manna demands exceptional wrist dorsiflexion — build gradually from V-sit.

divergence_notes: GB/OG use long L-sit/V-sit holds before manna; FF often cycles compression drills daily.

common_faults: Only hinging at hips without spinal flexion

timeline.from_level: 30s floor L-sit, pike fold with chest to thighs, 30s ring support hold
timeline.human_label: V-sit roughly 1–2.5 years from a solid L-sit; a full manna is 4–9+ years and many athletes never achieve it
timeline.notes: The longest tree in the library and the one where individual variation is most extreme. OG2 places the manna at the very top of the compression chart. Progress is gated by shoulder-extension range and posterior-chain flexibility at least as much as by compression strength, and passive hip and shoulder structure varies enough that some athletes plateau permanently. Treated as `estimated` throughout — no source publishes manna timelines.

variance_drivers.note: Straight-arm and pulling skills scale roughly with bodyweight at a fixed height. Athletes above ~85 kg routinely sit at the top of every band; lighter athletes at the bottom. This is the single largest driver on lever and planche trees.

Rate of adaptation is logarithmic. An athlete with 3+ years of consistent resistance training moves through early steps in a fraction of the listed time but gains little advantage on the last two steps of any tree.
Connective tissue remodels more slowly with age. Athletes over ~40 should read the upper half of every band and extend tendon-conditioning steps rather than compressing them.
Longer arms and legs lengthen the lever at a fixed bodyweight. Taller athletes commonly need one extra intermediate shape (one-leg before straddle) that shorter athletes can skip.
Below roughly 2 quality sessions per week most athletes stall indefinitely on advanced steps. Gains from going beyond 4–5 sessions per week are small and injury risk rises (arampatzis-2024-loading).
Video review or a coach correcting shape is repeatedly reported to roughly halve time-to-skill on balance-dominant work versus unguided practice (kyleweiger-handstand).

prerequisite_standards.name: Floor L-sit
prerequisite_standards.rationale: The entry shape for the whole tree.

prerequisite_standards.name: Pike fold
prerequisite_standards.rationale: Compression range gates the V-sit more often than compression strength does.

prerequisite_standards.name: Shoulder extension range
prerequisite_standards.target: hands behind hips, able to lift the body clear
prerequisite_standards.rationale: The manna is fundamentally a shoulder-extension problem. Without the range it is not achievable at any strength level.

plateau_signatures.signal: Legs will not rise above horizontal no matter how much hip-flexor work is added
typical_causes: Hamstring and lower-back compression range, not hip-flexor strength, is the limiter
Active compression never trained — only passive folds
resolution: Train active compression: seated leg lifts at end range, not passive stretching
Add pike fold work in parallel with the strength work

plateau_signatures.signal: No progress over a year or more despite consistent, well-executed practice
typical_causes: Insufficient shoulder-extension range — often a structural limit rather than a training one
Attempting the manna before owning a full V-sit
resolution: Spend a dedicated block on loaded shoulder extension
Reassess honestly whether this is a realistic goal; many lifelong practitioners never achieve a full manna

regression_triggers.trigger: Layoff or markedly reduced training for less than 4 weeks (illness, travel, work crunch)
regression_triggers.typical_dropback: No step lost. Hold times commonly return 10–25% short for the first two sessions; eccentric control and shape quality degrade before maximal strength does.
regression_triggers.action: Resume one step below your unlock for two sessions, then retest. Do not re-earn the whole step — strength-trained athletes show only limited decline at this timescale.

regression_triggers.typical_dropback: Force production falls roughly 7–12%, which usually costs one step on hold-based progressions and one to two steps on the hardest dynamic ones. Recently acquired gains are retained far better than the loss in maximal force suggests.
regression_triggers.action: Restart two steps below your previous unlock and rebuild with full volume but reduced intensity. Expect to regain the lost steps in a fraction of the time they originally took.

regression_triggers.trigger: Planned deload, or four consecutive weeks with no measurable progress
regression_triggers.typical_dropback: None. Hold times often improve in the week after the deload.
regression_triggers.action: Cut volume roughly in half and keep intensity, for one week. Overcoming Gravity's rule is that four weeks without progress means the cycle is finished, not that you need to try harder.

regression_triggers.trigger: Tendon pain forcing modified or stopped training
regression_triggers.typical_dropback: Highly variable. Time lost is usually 6–12 weeks because the tissue must be reloaded from a low baseline, and the affected step is typically lost entirely.
regression_triggers.action: Drop to the last pain-free step, reintroduce isometric then slow eccentric loading, and rebuild across at least 8–12 weeks — the window in which tendon stiffness actually changes. Returning at the previous intensity is the most common cause of recurrence.

injury_risk_timeline.mechanism: Bodyweight supported at end-range shoulder extension with straight arms — a position most adults cannot passively achieve, let alone load
prophylaxis: Build passive then loaded shoulder-extension range across at least 12 weeks before any manna shape
Use parallettes to reduce the extension demand
red_flags: Front-of-shoulder pain in the support position
Loss of extension range between sessions

injury_risk_timeline.mechanism: Active compression at end range with the hamstrings lengthened and the hip flexors contracting hard against them
prophylaxis: Warm up compression range before loading it
Progress hold time before progressing leg height
red_flags: Proximal hamstring tenderness at the sit bone

injury_risk_timeline.mechanism: Extreme lumbar and thoracic extension combined with compression load
prophylaxis: Distribute extension through the thoracic spine rather than the lumbar
Stop when the position is achieved by lumbar hinging
red_flags: Localised lumbar pain in the manna shape

productive.notes: Higher frequency than the lever trees because much of the work is range-and-position rather than maximal force. Keep individual sets short.

too_much_signals: Compression range worse at the start of a session than the previous one

deload.protocol: One week of unloaded range work and L-sit holds only.
deload.trigger: Range regression, or six weeks without progress.
